analysis.one_liner: Forces mortgage relief for homeowners in foreclosure and restricts dividends and pay at banks taking bailout money.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of 2008 amid the foreclosure crisis, the bill was referred to two House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Three weeks after Congress passed the $700 billion bank bailout, this bill would have changed it. It would have required — instead of merely encouraged — government-held mortgage holders and servicers to modify loans and use the HOPE for Homeowners program to stop foreclosures. It would have let families in foreclosure reduce their mortgage debt in bankruptcy, waived credit counseling for them, and limited late fees. To protect taxpayers, banks that sold assets to the Treasury would have been barred from raising dividends and would have had to cut dividends by any executive pay above $500,000 per officer.
analysis.who_benefits: Families in foreclosure who could not otherwise keep their homes: the bill let them rewrite their mortgage in bankruptcy to an amount they could actually pay, wiped out the pre-bankruptcy credit counseling requirement, and stopped lenders from piling fees on them during the case. It also required lenders to participate in the HOPE for Homeowners program whenever a homeowner applied, and required managers of government-held mortgage assets to modify loans rather than merely suggest it. Taxpayers who funded the bank rescue gained dividend limits and a pay penalty on bailout banks.

how_it_helps.text: Changed three words in the bailout law from 'encourage' to 'require,' so that Treasury and federal managers holding mortgages or mortgage-backed securities had to force loan modifications and use the HOPE for Homeowners program to prevent avoidable foreclosures.

Let a bankruptcy judge reduce a family's mortgage debt on their primary home when their income could not both cover the old payment and keep the home, paying the lender over up to 40 years at a market-based rate.

Waived the credit counseling requirement for anyone whose home was in scheduled foreclosure, and barred debtors from liability for lender fees that arose during the bankruptcy case unless the lender gave timely notice and the fees were lawful and reasonable.

Barred banks that sold assets to Treasury from paying higher cumulative dividends than before the sale until Treasury no longer held the assets, and required a dividend cut equal to each senior executive's pay above $500,000.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and servicers would take losses on loans reduced in bankruptcy and lose foreclosure-related fees; banks that sold assets to Treasury under the bailout would lose the ability to raise dividends and would have to cut dividends to cover executive pay above $500,000.

drawbacks.text: Lenders recover less: the bankruptcy provision pays mortgage holders over up to 40 years at a fixed conventional-mortgage rate plus a risk premium, which gives banks less than the original contract and gives them standing grounds to argue that bankruptcy-based loan relief raises mortgage rates for everyone else.

The bill would bar claims for damages or rescission to be disallowed even after a foreclosure judgment when based on violations of the Truth in Lending Act or other consumer protection laws, which could reopen finished foreclosures and generate litigation for mortgage holders.

The dividend freeze applies to any bank that sold assets to Treasury, not just underperforming ones, which banks argued would discourage healthy institutions from joining the rescue program and slow recapitalization of the banking system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and targeted: in late 2008 foreclosures were the core of the crisis, and the bill attacked it directly by making mortgage relief mandatory rather than voluntary and giving bankruptcy courts the same power over home loans they already had over vacation homes. The costs fall on mortgage lenders and on banks receiving public money, which is why it would have been hard-fought; the bill's mechanism of paying reduced claims over decades is designed to avoid sudden bank losses. The main honest criticism is that after-the-fact claim reopening and across-the-board dividend freezes could have had side effects on credit availability, but on balance the bill shifted risk from homeowners and taxpayers back to the institutions that caused the crisis.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services and Judiciary committees from the day it was introduced in late November 2008 until that Congress ended in early January 2009 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Hodes (D-NH) and five other House Democrats introduced the bill on November 20, 2008, three weeks after the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act — the $700 billion bank bailout — became law.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Financial Services Committee and additionally to the House Judiciary Committee.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.
The bill's core idea — allowing bankruptcy judges to reduce mortgage principal on primary homes — resurfaced the next Congress and again failed to become law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and the financial institutions that received bailout money were better off: no dividend freeze, no pay penalty, and no mandatory loan modifications — government mortgage relief stayed voluntary. Struggling homeowners gained nothing; foreclosures continued at crisis rates into 2009 and 2010.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, but its entire support was Democratic — 9 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican — and no committee took action under majority control.

industries.note: The bill forced them into loan modifications and HOPE for Homeowners participation whenever a homeowner applied, stripped their ability to collect fees arising during a bankruptcy, and let bankruptcy judges reduce principal on home loans. Their gains come from collecting payments and fees on loans ordinary families are trying to save.

industries.industry: Financial institutions receiving bailout assets from Treasury
industries.note: They would have been barred from raising cumulative dividends while Treasury held their troubled assets and would have had to cut dividends by every dollar of senior executive pay above $500,000. The same public money they received would have come with those strings.

Federal property managers would have been required to modify underlying loans even when holding only an interest in pooled obligations, reducing the cash flow on the securities — though the modifications were aimed at preventing foreclosures, which destroy the collateral value entirely.
